p: A watchman stood on a wall or tower and sounded the alarm; Ezekiel is told he is one.
b: The tsofeh was a lookout posted on a city wall, a tower or a border to see an enemy coming and blow the horn. Here the picture starts as a normal custom of any land, then turns (33:7) to the prophet. Other prophets use the same image: Habakkuk waits at his watch post (Habakkuk 2:1), Jeremiah says the LORD set watchmen over the people (Jeremiah 6:17), and Hosea calls the prophet a watchman and then complains that he meets traps (Hosea 9:8). Isaiah has bad watchmen who are blind dogs (Isaiah 56:10) and good ones who shout for joy at the LORD's return (Isaiah 52:8).

t: The people of the land ('am ha'arets)
p: The phrase names different groups in different passages; here it is the citizens who choose the watchman.
b: 'Am ha'arets, 'the people of the land', is not one fixed group. In Kings it is the landowning citizens who act together in a crisis: they crown Joash and Josiah and take Jehoahaz (2 Kings 11:14; 21:24; 23:30). In Ezekiel it can be the ordinary population that the leaders oppress (22:29) or whose hands go weak (7:27). In Ezra 4:4 it is the neighboring peoples who oppose the returned exiles, and in later rabbinic Hebrew an 'am ha'arets is a person who does not keep the law carefully (Mishnah, Avot 2:5). Here, in 33:2, it is the citizens of a land under threat, who choose their own lookout. In 39:13 the same phrase names the whole population, who bury the dead. The Plain English Translation says 'the people of the land' every time.

p: The Hebrew says 'from their ends'; the people pick a watchman from their border or from among themselves.
b: The Hebrew is miqtsehem, literally 'from their end(s)'. Two readings are possible. It can mean from the edge of their territory, where a lookout would stand (the Plain English Translation; the KJV's 'of their coasts' is the same reading). Or it can mean 'from among their number', picking one man from the whole body. The sense is the same either way: the people themselves choose the man, which makes his duty a trust they gave him, not only an order from above.

p: The shofar was a ram's horn, the alarm of ancient Israel.
b: A shofar is a horn, usually a ram's. It gave signals in war and peace: an alarm when the enemy came (Jeremiah 6:1), a call to arms (Nehemiah 4:18-20) and, in Amos, the sign that no city could ignore (Amos 3:6). The site renders it 'ram's horn', as in Jeremiah 42:14 (the people who will not 'hear the sound of the ram's horn' in Egypt). The sword and the horn are a pair throughout this chapter.

a: his blood will rest on his own head
p: A legal saying: the person who ignores a warning bears the blame for his own death.
b: 'His blood on his head' is a court formula for the person who must answer for a death. It frees others from blame when the man brought it on himself, as in Joshua 2:19 and 2 Samuel 1:16. Here it works twice. The one who ignores the horn carries his own blood (33:4-5). The watchman who never blew it carries the blood of the one who died (33:6, 8). The point of 33:4-6 is who is to blame, not who will die.

a: I have appointed you as watchman over the house of Israel
p: These words repeat 3:17-19; the call is renewed on the eve of the city's fall.
b: Ezekiel 33:7-9 almost repeats his first commissioning (3:17-19), when he was sent to Israel's exiles. The difference is the moment. The first time came with the muteness of 3:26-27, which kept him from speaking except when the LORD gave him a word. Now, about to learn that the city has fallen (33:21-22), he gets the same charge again before his mouth opens for good. Paul uses watchman language of himself in Acts 20:26-27, and Hebrews 13:17 says church leaders 'keep watch' over souls.

p: The verb means to rot or waste away, like a body, like the curse of Leviticus 26.
b: Namaq is 'to rot, waste away'. Leviticus 26:39 uses it of survivors who will 'rot' in their enemies' lands because of their guilt, and Ezekiel has used it before, of a people who will 'waste away' in their guilt (4:17; 24:23). The exiles quote the curse back to God as a description of themselves: they believe they are the Leviticus survivors, so they ask the right question, 'How can we go on living?' God's answer, in 33:11, is that the curse does not have the last word.

t: God swears by his own life
p: God takes an oath on his own life, and what he swears here is mercy, not threat.
b: Chai ani, 'as I live', is God's oath. He swears by his own life because nothing is greater to swear by (compare Numbers 14:21, 28). In Ezekiel the oath usually seals a threat (5:11; 14:16, 18, 20; 33:27; 34:8; 35:6, 11). Here it seals the opposite: God does not enjoy the death of anyone. The oath makes 33:11 one of the book's most solemn statements, and Ezekiel's hearers could not miss it.

a: I take no pleasure in the death of a wicked man
t: Does God want the wicked to die?
p: Churches read this and the matching 18:23, 32 differently, along with 2 Peter 3:9 and 1 Timothy 2:4.
b: Chafets means to delight in, to want, to be pleased with. The verse says the death of the wicked does not please God; what pleases him is that they turn and live (compare 18:23, 32; Lamentations 3:33). Readers ask whether God wants this for everyone. Many take it as a sincere wish for all people, and read it beside 2 Peter 3:9 and 1 Timothy 2:4. Others say it is spoken to Israel, the house addressed, in the setting of the exile. Churches that teach unconditional election read it with the distinction between God's revealed wish and his hidden plan. See the 'Where Christians differ' card on this chapter.

p: The main verb of repentance in the Hebrew Bible; this chapter has it ten times.
b: Shuv means to turn, to turn back, to return. It is the main word for repentance, and it also means to come home from exile, so 'Turn back!' carries both senses to the exiles. Counting the Hebrew word list, this chapter has the root ten times (33:9 twice, 11 three times, 12, 14, 15, 18 and 19). The double call recalls Jeremiah's pleas (Jeremiah 3:12, 14, 22) and Hosea 14:1-2.

a: cannot rescue him on that day
p: The chapter's 'live' and 'die' can mean surviving the sword, covenant life, or eternal life.
b: Commentators read the 'life' and 'death' of 33:12-20 in different ways. Some take them as survival or death in the coming disaster, which 33:27-29 supports: the ones in the ruins fall by sword and plague. Others read them as life within the covenant community. Christian readers since the Fathers have also heard the language of eternal life and death, and churches differ on whether a believer can finally fall away (see the topic on perseverance). Nothing in the verse says that a past righteous record is useless; the point is that a past record does not decide the present choice.

p: The phrase echoes Leviticus 18:5, where keeping God's rules is how a person 'lives'.
b: Ezekiel's phrase 'the rules of life' reflects Leviticus 18:5, the verse that says a person who keeps God's rules will live by them. Ezekiel quotes the idea again in 20:11, 13, 21. Paul quotes Leviticus 18:5 twice (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12) when he argues about law and faith. In Ezekiel the 'rules that give life' are not a ladder to earn God's love. They are the path the wicked man takes when he turns back, and the proof he has truly turned: he returns what he took.

a: way of the Lord is not fair
p: The charge, 'not level, not weighed rightly', is the one made in 18:25 and 18:29.
b: Tikken is 'to measure, to weigh out'. The exiles say God's scales are off, using the same complaint as in 18:25 and 18:29. In 1 Samuel 2:3 'deeds are weighed' by the LORD; Proverbs 16:2 has him weigh motives. Here the charge turns around: the uneven way is theirs. Abraham's question, 'Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is right?' (Genesis 18:25), is a good partner for this verse, and Paul meets the same charge in Romans 9:14.

p: About five or six months after the city fell, a refugee reaches Babylon; compare 24:26-27.
b: The Hebrew palit means someone who escaped. Ezekiel had been told he would hear the news this way (24:26-27), and that his mouth would open when it came (33:22). The city was breached in the fourth month and the Temple burned in the fifth month of 586 BC (2 Kings 25:3-9; Jeremiah 52:6-13). A tenth-month date puts the arrival five or six months later, which fits a journey of weeks or months (a large caravan took four months, Ezra 7:9). Some scholars date the fall to 587 BC; with the twelfth-year date the gap would then be about seventeen months, which is why some prefer the eleventh-year reading (see the variants).

p: The muteness of 3:26-27 and 24:27 ends; what it was is debated.
b: Lo ne'elamti 'od, 'I was dumb no more'. The silence was announced in 3:26-27 and promised to end in 24:27 and 33:22. Whether Ezekiel could not speak at all, or could speak only the LORD's words and not argue with the people or plead for them, is debated: 3:27 says he spoke only when the LORD opened his mouth. Older writers also tried medical diagnoses (catalepsy and the like); more recent commentators treat the silence as a role, a period in which he could not act as the people's intercessor. The release comes the evening before the news arrives (33:22).

p: The survivors argue that the land belongs to them because it was given to one man and they are many.
b: The argument runs from small to large: if one man, Abraham, received the land (Genesis 12:7; 17:8), those who are many surely own it now. Isaiah 51:2 also stresses that Abraham was one. Ezekiel had already heard a similar claim from Jerusalem's people about the exiles (11:15). Ezekiel does not deny Abraham's promise. He asks what kind of people claim it while eating blood, worshiping idols and killing (33:25-26), and he answers that they will not keep the land.

p: Ezekiel's word for idols is a mocking one, close to a word for dung pellets.
b: Gillulim appears about thirty-nine times in Ezekiel, far more than in any other book (compare Leviticus 26:30; 1 Kings 15:12). It sounds like galal, 'to roll', and may be related to gelel, 'dung pellets'; it is a word of contempt, not a neutral name. The Greek translates eidōla, 'idols'. This book keeps three Hebrew words apart: gillulim 'filthy idols', shiqqutsim 'detestable things' (37:23) and to'evot 'abhorrent things' (33:26, 29). The site's 1 Kings 15:12 also has 'filthy idols'.

a: meat with the blood still in it
p: The Torah forbids eating blood; the Hebrew phrase may also point to a ritual meal.
b: Eating meat with the blood is forbidden in Genesis 9:4 and Leviticus 17:10-14, because the blood is life. The Hebrew here, 'al hadam, 'over the blood', is the phrase of Leviticus 19:26, which sits next to a ban on divination. For that reason some commentators think this charge also names a ritual meal, perhaps a rite for the dead, and not only an ordinary breach of diet. In 1 Samuel 14:32-34 hungry soldiers eat meat with the blood, and Saul steps in to stop it.

p: Three of the book's judgments are named; compare the four in 14:21 and 5:12.
b: The sword, wild animals and plague (dever) are three of the four judgments of 14:21, where famine is the fourth, and they echo the plague, famine and sword of 5:12. Leviticus 26:22-25 is their source: wild animals, sword and plague all come after the people break the covenant. For Ezekiel's hearers, the ones 'among the ruins' are the survivors of Judah, who think they have been spared and will take the land. The Plain English Translation uses 'plague' for dever everywhere in this book.

p: The Hebrew word 'agavim means desire or lust; the sense in this verse is disputed.
b: 'Agavim occurs in 33:31-32 and in Jeremiah 4:30. The root means sensual desire or lust ('agavah in Ezekiel 23; in Jeremiah 4:30 Jerusalem tries to attract lovers). Many translations soften it to 'love' (mouths full of love for the prophet's words). The Plain English Translation keeps the plain sense, 'passion', because the picture of 33:32 is a love song. The Greek reads something quite different, 'a lie in their mouth' (Swete's Codex Vaticanus), and the Hebrew in 33:31b is also hard. The sense in either case is the same: their talk is eager and their hearts are elsewhere.

p: The exiles come to Ezekiel's house for a good performance; they will not do what he says.
b: Ezekiel's neighbors treat his messages as an evening's pleasure, like a singer with a lovely voice. This fits what we know: he acted out signs (4:1-5:4), sang laments (19; 27; 32) and was called a maker of riddles (20:49). The elders came to his house to sit and hear him (8:1; 14:1; 20:1). Jesus makes the same charge against hearers who say 'Lord, Lord' and do not act (Luke 6:46) and James warns against hearing without doing (James 1:22-25). Ezekiel's own comment comes in 33:33: when it happens, they will know.

a: a prophet was in their midst
p: The same words close the call in 2:5; Deuteronomy 18:21-22 gives the test they now meet.
b: 'They will know that a prophet has been among them' repeats 2:5, at Ezekiel's call, so the book's middle opens with its beginning. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 says a prophet is known by whether his word comes true. When the news of 33:21 arrives, that test has been met. For the exiles who listened and did nothing, the lesson comes late. For the book's readers, it means that all the earlier warnings (chapters 4-24) are now confirmed history.

p: Hoy was the cry at a funeral; a prophet uses it to say someone is as good as dead.
b: Hoy is the cry of mourning at a funeral, 'Alas!' (1 Kings 13:30). A prophet uses it to open an accusation: 'Woe to those who...'. The words after it name the guilty. Here the guilty are Israel's shepherds, who have eaten the flock. Jeremiah began his own shepherd oracle with the same cry: "Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the flock of my pasture, the LORD declares." (Jeremiah 23:1). Ezekiel 34 can be read as a long development of that verse.

a: prophesy against the shepherds of Israel
p: In the ancient Near East 'shepherd' was a title for kings and officials, not only for farmers.
b: Mesopotamian and Egyptian kings called themselves shepherds of their people, and Israel used the same word for leaders: David is called to shepherd Israel (2 Samuel 5:2), and Jeremiah's shepherds (Jeremiah 2:8; 10:21; 23:1-4) are rulers and priests who failed. Ezekiel's 'shepherds' include the kings of Judah (Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Zedekiah) and the officials, priests and prophets who served with them (compare 22:25-28). Zechariah 10:3 and 11:4-17 reuse the image later. Because the shepherds are rulers, the good shepherd promised in 34:23 is a ruler too.
r: 2 Samuel 5:2; Jeremiah 2:8; Jeremiah 10:21; Jeremiah 23:1-4; Zechariah 10:3; Zechariah 11:4-17; 22:25-28

p: The Hebrew says 'fat'; the Greek, the Latin and others read 'milk'.
b: The Masoretic Text reads the three consonants chlb as cheleb, 'fat'; with other vowels they are chalav, 'milk', and the Greek (Swete) and the Latin Vulgate read 'milk', which fits the picture of sheep that give milk and wool. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew 'fat'. The sense is the same: the shepherds took the best of the flock for themselves. See the variant on this verse.

a: ruled them with force and with crushing cruelty
p: The word for 'crushing cruelty' is the one used of Egypt's slave labor in Exodus 1:13-14.
b: Perekh, 'crushing cruelty', is a rare word. It is the word used of the Egyptians' cruel work on the Hebrew slaves in Exodus 1:13-14, and Leviticus 25:43, 46, 53 forbids using it against an Israelite slave. By choosing it, Ezekiel says Israel's shepherds are acting like Pharaoh's taskmasters over God's own flock. The five kinds of sheep the shepherds ignored (weak, sick, broken, strayed, lost) are the people a leader is meant to protect.

p: 'Sheep without a shepherd' is a standing picture of leaderless Israel.
b: Moses asks for a successor so the community will not be 'like sheep that have no shepherd' (Numbers 27:17), and the prophet Micaiah sees Israel scattered 'like sheep without a shepherd' (1 Kings 22:17). Jesus uses the phrase when he sees the crowds (Matthew 9:36; Mark 6:34). For Ezekiel the lack is not that there are no leaders; there are shepherds, but they feed themselves, so the flock has no shepherd in any real sense.

a: As surely as I live, the Lord GOD declares: my flock has become prey
t: An oath with a long middle
p: The Hebrew oath begins but runs on for several clauses before it ends in 34:10.
b: The Hebrew has the oath-formula 'as I live... if not (im lo)', which means 'surely'. The long reason runs on through the verse (the flock became prey, no shepherd searched), and the result comes in 34:10 ('Here I am against the shepherds'). English cannot hold a sentence this long, so the Plain English Translation breaks it into short sentences. The reason for the judgment is that the shepherds did not search for the flock.

a: I will search for my flock myself
p: The LORD takes over the work the shepherds neglected; the image runs through the Psalms and John 10.
b: God as Israel's shepherd goes back to Jacob's blessing (Genesis 48:15). Psalm 23:1 says: "The LORD is my shepherd; / I will never be in need." (Psalm 23:1). Isaiah 40:11 and Jeremiah 31:10 promise he will gather the scattered flock. Jesus claims the picture in John 10:11-16 ('I am the good shepherd') and in the story of the lost sheep (Luke 15:3-7). Peter calls Jesus the 'Shepherd and Overseer' of souls (1 Peter 2:25) and tells elders to be examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:2-4). The Roman Catholic lectionary reads Ezekiel 34:11-12, 15-17 on the Feast of Christ the King, Year A.
r: Genesis 48:15; Psalm 23:1; Isaiah 40:11; Jeremiah 31:10; Luke 15:3-7; John 10:11-16; 1 Peter 2:25; 1 Peter 5:2-4

a: a day of cloud and thick darkness
t: A day of cloud and darkness
p: This phrase comes from the day of the LORD: Joel and Zephaniah use it of judgment.
b: 'A day of cloud and thick darkness' is the language of the day of the LORD in Joel 2:2 and Zephaniah 1:15. Ezekiel uses it of the day the flock was scattered, which means the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC: the day of judgment on the shepherds was also the day the sheep were driven out. God promises to rescue them from that very day. The same scene reappears in 30:3 ('a day of cloud') for Egypt.

a: The lost one I will look for.
p: The four kinds of weak sheep in 34:4 become four promises of the LORD.
b: Verse 4 listed the sheep the shepherds ignored; verse 16 lists what the LORD will do for each. Luke's shepherd who leaves ninety-nine and searches until he finds one (Luke 15:4-6) and Jesus' saying that the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10) echo this verse. The last line is the grim one: the fat and the strong sheep, who pushed others aside, are judged (34:17-22). The Hebrew says 'I will destroy', as the Plain English Translation does; some witnesses read 'I will watch over'. See the variant.

a: between the rams and the male goats
p: Within the flock, the rams and male goats are the strong who push the weak.
b: The leaders of the flock are also the leaders of a herd. Zechariah 10:3 calls Judah's rulers 'shepherds' and 'male goats' ('attudim) in one breath, and Isaiah 14:9 uses the same word for the dead leaders of the earth in Sheol. Ezekiel's judgment now shifts from the shepherds to the fat sheep among the flock themselves (34:17-22): those who took the best pasture, trampled the grass and muddied the water. Matthew 25:31-33, where the Son of Man separates sheep from goats, is often compared.

p: Jewish readers expect a king from David's line; Christians read it of Jesus, the good shepherd.
b: David had been dead for about four hundred years. 'My servant David' means a king of David's line, as 2 Samuel 7:16 promised. Jewish tradition reads this as the Messiah son of David; the Talmud debates whether he will be a new David or David himself (Sanhedrin 98b). The Gospel of John has Jesus say 'I am the good shepherd' (John 10:11) and speak of 'one flock, one shepherd' (John 10:16), which echoes this verse and 37:24. Critical scholars often read the line as a promise that the Davidic house will return, not as a single end-time figure. See also the note at 37:24.

p: The KJV and many versions say 'prince'; the site says 'leader', a ruler under the LORD.
b: Nasi means someone lifted up, a chief or leader. The KJV and many modern versions say 'prince', which suggests a king's son; the site renders it 'leader'. In Ezekiel the word stresses that David's heir rules under the LORD, who is the real shepherd: in 34:23 he is a shepherd, in 34:24 a nasi, and in 37:22, 24 a king. The Greek has archōn ('ruler') in each place. The same word is used for Israel's leader in the Temple chapters (45-46).

p: The covenant of peace removes the wild animals and ends the curse of Leviticus 26.
b: Berit shalom is a covenant of wholeness and safety. God gave one to Phinehas (Numbers 25:12) and promises one to Zion (Isaiah 54:10). Here it undoes the curse: Leviticus 26:6 promises that God will remove wild animals from the land when the people obey, and Ezekiel 14:15, 21 had listed wild animals as a judgment. The covenant is made with 'them', the flock, not with David alone (the Greek has 'with David'). The same phrase returns in 37:26.

p: The picture comes from Leviticus 26:13, where God broke the bars of Egypt's yoke.
b: In Leviticus 26:13 God reminds Israel that he broke 'the bars of your yoke' when he brought them out of Egypt. Ezekiel puts a second exodus on top of the first. The people are again a yoked team, this time to Babylon, and the LORD will break the bars again. The same hope is behind 20:33-44 (a second wilderness march) and Jeremiah 28:2-4 (the false prophet Hananiah's promise to break the yoke, which Jeremiah says is false).

p: The Hebrew says a planting for renown; the Greek says a planting 'of peace'.
b: Matta' leshem, 'a planting for a name', is a fruitful garden famous for its renown, in contrast to the land that is devoured by famine. The Hebrew word means something planted, and Isaiah 60:21 and 61:3 use it of God's people as his planting. The Greek (Swete) has 'a plant of peace' (phyton eirēnēs), perhaps from reading shalom for shem. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; see the variant.

p: The metaphor ends with a plain statement: the sheep are people.
b: The last line drops the picture: 'You are human (adam), and I am your God.' It is a quiet reminder that the flock is a human people, with a Shepherd who is God. In the Hebrew, 'human' (adam) also echoes the ground (adamah), the land that 36:17 and 36:24 are about. Ezekiel's usual title for himself, 'son of man', is the same word again.

t: Seir, the hill country of Edom
p: Seir is Edom's mountain home, the land of Esau's descendants south of the Dead Sea.
b: Mount Seir is the hill country south and east of the Dead Sea, home of the Edomites, descendants of Jacob's brother Esau (Genesis 36:8-9; Deuteronomy 2:5). Ezekiel has already spoken against Edom's revenge (25:12-14), and Obadiah, Psalm 137:7 and Lamentations 4:21-22 charge Edom with helping at Jerusalem's fall. Commentators generally read chapter 35 with 36:1-15 as a pair: Seir, the mountain that took Israel's land, is judged; the mountains of Israel, which were looted, are restored.
r: 25:12-14; Genesis 36:8-9; Deuteronomy 2:5; Obadiah 10-14; Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21-22; Malachi 1:2-5

p: The hatred between Edom and Israel went back to Jacob and Esau.
b: 'Eivat 'olam, 'hatred of ancient times', points back to the quarrel of Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25-27) and Edom's refusal to let Israel pass in the wilderness (Numbers 20:14-21). Later Edom took advantage of Judah's weakness (2 Kings 8:20-22; Amos 1:11; Obadiah 10-14). The Hebrew calls the time of Jerusalem's fall an 'end of guilt', the moment when the people's guilt had run its full course, and the Plain English Translation follows it with 'final punishment'.
r: Genesis 25:22-26; Genesis 27:41; Numbers 20:14-21; 2 Kings 8:20-22; Amos 1:11; Obadiah 10-14

a: I will appoint you for blood, and blood will chase you
p: The Hebrew puns on dam (blood) and Edom (and adom, red).
b: The Hebrew sounds like Edom's name: dam 'blood' and 'adom 'red' are close to 'Edom, and Genesis 25:25, 30 plays on the same red in Esau's story. Ezekiel's sentence says the nation that loved shedding blood will be pursued by blood: a death-penalty rule applied to a nation (Genesis 9:6; Numbers 35:19). English cannot hold the sound-play, so the note carries it.

p: Edom's boast is answered by a short clause that anticipates the last words of the book.
b: 'The two nations and the two lands' are Israel and Judah, the two kingdoms that were once one (37:22). Edom meant to seize both. The closing clause, 'the LORD was there' (YHWH shammah hayah), is almost the name of the new city in 48:35, YHWH shammah, 'The LORD Is There'. Edom thought it was taking empty land; the LORD had never left it. The Greek has 'and the LORD is there'.

a: When the entire earth is celebrating
p: The verse can mean the world celebrates Edom's fall, or Edom celebrates while the earth does.
b: The Hebrew is short: 'when all the earth rejoices, desolation I make you'. Readers take it three ways: while the whole world rejoices at God's justice, Edom will be desolate (the Plain English Translation); as all the earth rejoiced over Israel's fall, so Edom will be treated; or while Edom rejoices, the earth is full of joy as Edom falls. The next verse, 35:15, supports the second: 'as you rejoiced... so I will do to you'.

p: The land was taken by Nabateans; Edomites became Idumeans; one forced conversion made them Judeans.
b: Edom lost its heartland to the Nabateans in the Persian period, and Edomites moved west into southern Judea, called Idumea. About 125 BC the Hasmonean John Hyrcanus forced them to be circumcised and join the Jewish people, according to Josephus (Antiquities 13.257-258). The family of Herod the Great came from Idumea. Malachi 1:2-5 already says Edom's land is a ruin. Prophecy and history agree on Edom's fall as a nation, though not on every detail.

t: The same address, a new message
p: Chapter 6 told these mountains they would be judged; chapter 36 tells them they will be restored.
b: Ezekiel's first oracle to the land was to the same hearers: 'set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them' (6:2-3). That speech was judgment on the high places and altars. Now the same address brings a promise. The mountains are personified, as in Micah 6:1-2, and are the audience for what is really said to the exiles. The next fifteen verses answer two things the mountains suffered: the enemy's claim (36:2) and the nations' mockery (36:3-4).

p: Bamot usually means 'high places', the sites of worship; the word is a pun and a charge.
b: Bamot means hills or heights, and in Israel's history it was the name of the hilltop shrines (6:3). Ezekiel makes a bitter pun on it in 20:29. The enemy here calls the hills 'ancient heights' that now 'belong to us', which can mean Israel's old hills or the old Canaanite shrines that Edom and the other nations claimed. The word is one of several that recall the first oracle of chapter 6 in this chapter's opening.

a: In the fire of my jealousy
p: One Hebrew root is both 'jealousy' and 'zeal': God's fierce commitment to his people and his name.
b: Qin'ah is the burning loyalty of a spouse who will not share a beloved with another. It is God's attitude toward idolatry (Exodus 20:5; 34:14; Ezekiel 8:3-5), and it also turns against the nations who treat his people as loot (36:5-6; 35:11; 38:19). The same root gives 'I will be zealous for my holy name' in 39:25. It is not a petty feeling; in Ezekiel it is the heat of a God who will not let his honor or his people be taken.

a: so that its pastureland would become loot
p: Migrash can be 'pastureland' or 'a driving out'; both fit the Edomites' seizure.
b: The Hebrew migrash usually means a pasture or open land around a town (Numbers 35:2-5). It also comes from garash, 'to drive out', so some translate 'to drive it out as plunder'. The Plain English Translation takes 'pastureland' as a normal word for the open land the enemies wanted.

a: I have raised my hand and sworn
t: The oath with a raised hand
p: Lifting the hand was the gesture of a solemn oath; God swears to his people and against their enemies.
b: The Hebrew is 'I lifted up my hand', the gesture of an oath. God swore with a raised hand to give Israel the land (Exodus 6:8; Ezekiel 20:5-6, 15, 23, 28, 42; 47:14), and he raised his hand to scatter them in the wilderness (Numbers 14:30; Ezekiel 20:15, 23). Here the oath goes against the nations: they who made Israel bear insults will bear their own. It is the opposite side of the same oath-making.

t: A land that eats its people
p: The nations' saying about the land echoes the spies' report in Numbers 13:32.
b: In Numbers 13:32 the spies report that the land 'eats its inhabitants'. Here the nations say to the mountains, 'You devour people, and you have left your nations childless' (36:13), and God replies that this will end (36:14-15). The saying makes the land itself the culprit in Israel's losses. The LORD answers by repopulating it. The verb shakkel 'make childless' recurs in 36:12-15, with a textual problem in 36:14-15 (see the variant).

a: as unclean as a woman during her monthly period
p: The simile uses the ritual impurity of Leviticus 15, which was not a moral fault.
b: The Hebrew niddah is the state of a woman during her period, which made her ritually unclean for a time (Leviticus 15:19-24; 18:19; 20:18). That uncleanness was not a sin, and it carried no shame for her; it was a rule about contact with the holy. Ezekiel uses it as the image of a defilement the whole people caused to the land (36:17; compare Leviticus 18:24-28). Many readers feel the comparison is harsh, and some modern commentators say it should be read within priestly ideas of purity and not as a general judgment on women.

t: The name in the nations' mouths
p: Israel's exile makes the nations think the LORD is weak; Moses, the prophets and the psalmists all argue from this.
b: To 'profane' (chillel) the name is to treat it as common (Leviticus 22:32). The people's defeat and exile led the nations to say the LORD could not keep his own people in his own land. Moses used this argument to turn God from destroying Israel (Numbers 14:13-16; Deuteronomy 9:28), and the psalmist prays 'for the sake of your name' (Psalm 79:9-10; 106:8). Ezekiel makes the argument God's own: he will act, and not for Israel's sake (36:22), but to show who he is. Isaiah 48:9-11 says nearly the same.
r: Leviticus 22:32; Numbers 14:13-16; Deuteronomy 9:28; Psalm 79:9-10; Psalm 106:8; Isaiah 48:9-11; 20:9, 14, 22; Romans 2:24

a: I am not about to act for your sake
p: A statement of pure grace: God restores Israel for his own name, not for what they deserve.
b: The turn at 36:22 is one of the most radical lines in the book. Interpreters stress different things. Some hear grace without merit, a point easy to connect with Ephesians 2:8-9. Jewish readers read the passage as the heart of the Shabbat Parah haftarah (Ezekiel 36:16-38 for Ashkenazi communities, 36:16-36 for Sephardi) and tie it to the water of purification. Critical commentators note that the sentence answers the exiles' sense that God had been defeated: restoration will show who he is, not that Israel deserved it.

a: I will sprinkle pure water over you
p: The sprinkling of water recalls the water of Numbers 19 and is used in the New Testament for baptism.
b: The verb zaraq is also used for splashing the blood of sacrifices. Here it is water, and the nearest picture is the water of purification of Numbers 19:13, 20, made with the ashes of the red cow; the Shabbat Parah haftarah ties the two together. Psalm 51:7 asks for the same cleansing. The New Testament hears baptism: Hebrews 10:22 (bodies washed with pure water) and Titus 3:5-6. John 3:5 'born of water and the Spirit' is often set beside 36:25-27. Churches differ on whether the water is baptism; see the 'Where Christians differ' card.
orig: וְזָרַקְתִּי עֲלֵיכֶם מַיִם טְהוֹרִים (vezaraqti 'aleikhem mayim tehorim)
r: Numbers 19:13; Numbers 19:20; Psalm 51:7; Hebrews 10:22; John 3:5; Titus 3:5-6

t: The heart (lev) is the mind and will
p: In Hebrew the heart is the place of thought and choice; a heart of stone cannot be moved.
b: Lev, 'heart', is the center of a person: thinking, deciding and wanting, not only feeling. A stone heart is stubborn and cannot respond (3:7; 11:19). The promise runs through the prophets and the Law: God will circumcise the heart ("The LORD your God will circumcise your heart, and your descendants' hearts too" (Deuteronomy 30:6)), give a new heart (11:19-20; Psalm 51:10) and write his law there (Jeremiah 31:33). Ezekiel 18:31 puts the same demand as a command: 'make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit'. Here it is God's gift. Both appear in the book, and churches harmonize them differently.

p: The 'new spirit' here and 'my own Spirit' in 36:27 are the one Hebrew word, ruach.
b: Ruach means spirit, breath or wind. In 36:26 the 'new spirit' is a renewed human spirit, the person's inner life. In 36:27 'my own Spirit' is God's. The two are one word in Hebrew, and the Plain English Translation capitalizes the second because it is God's own. Nearby, in 37:5-14, the same word is the breath that brings the dry bones to life. The reader who follows this word from 36:26 to 37:14 sees a single idea: God's breath within, which makes a lifeless people alive.

t: The Spirit and the new covenant
p: Ezekiel promises God's Spirit in the heart, as Jeremiah promises the law written there.
b: Jeremiah promised: "I will put my law inside them, and on their hearts I will write it." (Jeremiah 31:33). Ezekiel promises the Spirit as the means, and the result is the same: people who walk in God's ways. Ezekiel 36 does not use the word 'covenant', but it gives the covenant formula (36:28) and the same inner change that Jeremiah's new covenant promises. In the New Testament, John 3:5-10 has Jesus tell Nicodemus, 'a teacher of Israel', to know this; Paul speaks of hearts of flesh in 2 Corinthians 3:3 and of walking by the Spirit in Romans 8:4; Titus 3:5-6 links washing and the Spirit.
r: Jeremiah 31:33; Jeremiah 31:31-34; John 3:5; John 3:10; Romans 8:4; 2 Corinthians 3:3; Titus 3:5-6

a: You will be my people, and I will be your God.
p: The sentence is the shortest summary of God's covenant with Israel.
b: 'You will be my people, and I will be your God' sums up the covenant. Leviticus 26:12 first states it; Jeremiah 24:7 and 31:33 repeat it; Ezekiel returns to it in 11:20, 14:11, 37:23 and 37:27. The New Testament applies the formula to the church in 2 Corinthians 6:16 and Revelation 21:3. The line is also the last sentence in the Hebrew promise of Ezekiel 36:24-28: gathering, cleansing, new heart and Spirit, then life in the land with God.

p: The ruined land will look like the garden of Eden: a first-days image for a new beginning.
b: Garden of Eden imagery appears again for a restored land in Isaiah 51:3 ('he will make her wilderness like Eden') and in reverse in Joel 2:3 (land like Eden before the army, a desert after). The same prophet uses Eden for the trees of the Pit in chapter 31 and for the king of Tyre in chapter 28. Here it means fruitfulness and peace, undoing the 'desolation' that this chapter keeps naming. Revelation 22:1-5 completes the picture.

p: God has promised, yet says he will let himself be asked.
b: The Hebrew verb is darash, 'to seek, to ask', here in the form 'I will let myself be sought' (iddaresh). God has just promised everything, and still says Israel will ask. This is a common biblical pairing: the promise does not replace prayer; it gives prayer something to hold (Jeremiah 29:12-14; Daniel 9:2-3; Luke 11:9-13).

p: Ruach is Spirit, breath and wind; the chapter plays on all three, and English cannot.
b: Ruach means wind, breath and spirit, and chapter 37 uses all three in a few verses. In 37:1 it is the Spirit of the LORD that carries Ezekiel. In 37:5-10 it is the breath that the bones lack and receive. In 37:9 the four ruchot are the four winds. In 37:14 it is God's own Spirit. The Plain English Translation keeps 'breath' in 37:5-10, 'winds' for the four directions and 'Spirit' where God is meant, and this note carries the play. Genesis 2:7 has God breathe a different word (neshamah) into the first man. John 3:8 plays on the same double sense in Greek (pneuma).

a: in the middle of a valley
p: The same word for 'valley' (biq'ah) is where Ezekiel saw the glory in 3:22-23 and 8:4.
b: The Hebrew biq'ah is a broad plain or valley. Ezekiel was told to go out to such a plain, where the glory of the LORD stood (3:22-23), and he saw the glory there again (8:4). So the valley of the bones is a place where God has already met him. It is not named, and nothing in the text puts it near a battle. Its bones are those of people 'killed' (37:9), not of the ordinary dead, and are left unburied, a shame (Jeremiah 8:1-2).

t: A vision, a parable or a promise of resurrection?
p: The meaning of the dry bones is the most-discussed question in the chapter.
b: The vision explains itself in 37:11: 'these bones are the whole house of Israel' and the graves are the exile. Most readers see a promise of the nation's return, and Jewish and Christian traditions both also hear resurrection of the dead. The Talmud records the debate: one rabbi says the dead stood, sang and died again, another says it was a parable, another says they went to Israel and had children (Sanhedrin 92b). The Targum is reported to read the chapter as a prophecy of the resurrection (Levey, 1987). Church fathers such as Tertullian cite it for bodily resurrection, and Jerome reads it of both the nation and the body; many Protestant commentators stress the renewal of the people or the church. Levenson argues that restoring Israel and raising the dead were close ideas, not rivals.

p: The bones are rebuilt in order, like a body being made, and breath comes last.
b: The order is sinews (gidim), flesh, skin, then breath, with a pause after the skin: the bodies lie complete and still (37:8). It is a picture of making a person. Job 10:11 says God 'clothed' the body with skin and flesh and 'knit' it with bones and sinews, and Psalm 139:13-16 describes the making of a body in the womb. Genesis 2:7 also has a body first and breath after. The two-step process of 37:7-10 suggests that nothing in Ezekiel's story is automatic: first the word makes the body, then a second word brings the breath.

t: A rattling, a roar, an earthquake
p: Ra'ash can be a rattle, a rumble or an earthquake; the Greek has 'earthquake'.
b: Ra'ash is any loud shaking noise: rattling, rumbling, the sound of a wheel (3:13), an earthquake. The Greek (Swete) reads seismos, 'earthquake'. The same word appears for the earthquake that shakes the land when Gog attacks (38:19). A dry rattle of bones joining is the simplest picture here, but the word's wider range suggests that something at God's command shook the whole valley.

t: Not only the dead, but the killed
p: The bones belong to people who were killed, as in a war.
b: The Hebrew haruggim means people who were killed, slain, not just dead. The picture is of a battlefield with unburied bodies. In the book's setting, the exiles have lost the war that ended in 586 BC; their own sense of being 'cut off' (37:11) matches the picture of the slain left in the open. Ezekiel's own people were not in graves, which is why 37:12 speaks of opening them: the exile is the grave.

p: The people's cry sounds like the laments in Psalm 88 and Lamentations.
b: The cry 'Our bones are dried up, our hope has vanished, we have been cut away' belongs with the laments. Psalm 88:5 speaks of those 'cut off' from God's hand, Lamentations 3:18 says 'my hope has perished from the LORD', and Lamentations 3:54 'I am cut off'. Bones drying up is a figure of strength drained (Proverbs 17:22). The exiles speak for themselves in these words, and Ezekiel was sent to answer them.

a: I will lift you out of your graves
t: Graves: the exile or the resurrection?
p: The graves are literally the exile, and over time the words were read of rising from the dead.
b: The text says plainly that the graves are the exile and the return is a return to 'the land of Israel' (37:12-14). Other texts use grave language the same way: Isaiah 26:19 says: "Your dead will live! / My corpses will rise!" (Isaiah 26:19). Whether that is nation or people is argued, and Daniel 12:2 is widely taken as the first clear text of resurrection of individuals. By the first century the chapter was heard as resurrection (Revelation 11:11 echoes Ezekiel 37:5, 10; compare Matthew 27:52-53). John 5:25-29 (the dead in the tombs hear the voice and come out) and 1 Corinthians 15:51-52 (the dead raised at the last trumpet) are the New Testament texts churches most often read beside it. Churches still use it that way: the Roman Catholic lectionary reads 37:12-14 on the Fifth Sunday of Lent in Year A, the Orthodox include 37:1-14 in the Holy Saturday vespers, and the synagogue reads it on the Sabbath of Passover.
r: Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2; Hosea 6:1-3; Revelation 11:11; Matthew 27:52-53; John 5:25-29; 1 Corinthians 15:51-52

a: I will place my Spirit in you so that you live
p: The promise of 36:27 is repeated here, and again in 39:29: the Spirit is the center of the restoration.
b: God's Spirit in the people (37:14) is the third time the promise is made in this part: 36:27, 37:14, 39:29. Joel 2:28-29 pours the Spirit on all flesh, and Acts 2:17-18 claims it for Pentecost; Isaiah 32:15 and 44:3 speak of the Spirit poured out like water. 'I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will act' is the seal Ezekiel puts on a promise (17:24; 22:14; 36:36). It is a fixed phrase; the Plain English Translation keeps it the same each time.

p: The Hebrew 'ets means a piece of wood; it is not the word for a staff.
b: The Hebrew is 'ets, 'wood', not matteh 'staff' (as in Numbers 17:2-3, where each tribe has a staff). Many English versions say 'stick'. Others picture a writing board of wood, like the tablet of Isaiah 30:8 and Habakkuk 2:2, because Ezekiel writes on it. The Plain English Translation keeps the plain 'piece of wood', which fits either picture and the later image of joining the two end to end (37:17). The sign-act is the point, not the shape.

p: The two houses are Judah in the south and the northern tribes under Ephraim, split since Rehoboam.
b: 'Judah' is the southern kingdom with its Davidic kings. 'Joseph... Ephraim' is the northern kingdom (Israel), led by Ephraim, the largest tribe descended from Joseph. They split after Solomon (1 Kings 12:16-20) and Assyria ended the northern kingdom about 722 BC. Isaiah 11:13 had promised an end to the rivalry of Ephraim and Judah, and Jeremiah 31:6, 9, 18-20 speaks of Ephraim coming home. Ezekiel's sign gives the old hope a visible form, with a surprising result: the exiles from Judah are asked to see the northern tribes as partners.

a: make the two a single piece of wood
t: The two pieces of wood in later readings
p: Jewish and Christian commentators take them as Israel's reunion; Latter-day Saints read two scriptures.
b: The text explains the sign itself: God will take the Israelites from the nations and make them 'a single nation' under one king (37:21-22). Jewish and Christian commentators have read it as the reunion of Judah and the northern tribes, and many Christians also as Jews and Gentiles joined in Christ (compare Ephesians 2:14-16). The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints reads the two pieces as two records, the Bible (Judah) and the Book of Mormon (Joseph, Ephraim), that come together; its own texts connect them (2 Nephi 3:12; Doctrine and Covenants 27:5). This is the church's reading of the passage, not a scholarly proposal. Other readers point to 37:21-28 as the reason this cannot be about books: the sign is about people returning to the land.

p: The healing of the split after Solomon is the first goal of the sign.
b: The split of Israel into two kingdoms after Solomon was the first great wound of Israel's story as a nation (1 Kings 12). The promise here is that it will not be repeated, a vow in the strongest words ('never... again'). The idea of a reunited people runs through Hosea 1:11, Jeremiah 3:18 and 50:4-5 and Zechariah 10:6-10. Whether Ezekiel is describing a historical reunion in the days after the exile, or one that remains to be fulfilled, is a question that Jews and Christians answer differently.

p: Shiqqutsim, 'detestable things', is another of Ezekiel's three words for idolatry.
b: Shiqqutsim are things God hates because they offend his holiness: idol images and their rites (7:20; 11:18, 21; 20:7-8, 30). The Plain English Translation keeps this apart from gillulim, 'filthy idols', and to'evot, 'abhorrent things'. The three are listed together in 5:11 and 7:20. Here the first two come in a pair ('their filthy idols, their detestable things'); the verse says that none of these will pollute the people again.

p: David stands for a king of his line who rules for the LORD; Jewish and Christian traditions fill this in differently.
b: 'My servant David' is the title God gives to David in 2 Samuel 7 and to the future king in Jeremiah 30:9, 33:15-22 and here (34:23-24; 37:24-25). Judaism looks for a Messiah of David's line; the note on 34:23 gives the Talmud's debate on whether he is a new David. Christians read Jesus, son of David (Luke 1:32-33; Acts 13:22-23). Ezekiel calls the figure nasi, 'leader', in 34:24 and 37:25 but 'king' in 37:22 and 37:24, and critical commentators discuss whether the two titles come from different layers or are a deliberate pairing. The Temple chapters (45-46) assume a 'leader' who gives offerings, not a king.

p: The Hebrew says 'your fathers'; the Greek says 'their fathers'.
b: The Hebrew suddenly turns to the second person: 'your fathers (avoteikhem) lived'. It may be an address to the hearers, or an uncorrected slip. The Greek (Swete) has 'their fathers', the natural flow of the sentence, and many translations follow it. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew's 'your'. The land is the one God gave to Jacob, the ancestor of the whole people.

p: The phrase 'covenant of peace' of 34:25 now becomes a covenant 'for all time' (berit 'olam).
b: Berit 'olam is the 'everlasting covenant' of Noah (Genesis 9:16), Abraham (Genesis 17:7), David (2 Samuel 23:5) and Isaiah 55:3. Ezekiel 16:60 promised one too after the unfaithful wife's shame. The peace in 34:25 was about safety from wild beasts; here it is the covenant that holds all of the earlier promises together. Jeremiah 50:5 says: "by a covenant for all time / that will not be forgotten." (Jeremiah 50:5).

p: Mishkan is the word for the Tabernacle; God promises to live again among his people.
b: Mishkan is 'dwelling place', the Tabernacle's name in Exodus 25:8-9. Leviticus 26:11-12 promises God will set his dwelling among Israel and walk among them, and Ezekiel 37:26-28 repeats it with the sanctuary. The Temple of 40-48 is the visible form of this promise: the glory returns to it (43:1-5). John 1:14 says the Word 'dwelt' (Greek eskēnōsen, 'pitched his tent') among us, and Revelation 21:3 says the dwelling of God is with human beings.

a: Gog, of the land of Magog
p: Gog is a ruler of a land called Magog; later readers made both into world powers.
b: Gog is a person, and Magog is his land or people; Magog is a son of Japheth in Genesis 10:2. Meshech and Tubal were real peoples of eastern Anatolia (the Mushki and Tabal of Assyrian records) who traded with Tyre (27:13). Scholars have proposed Gyges (Gugu) of Lydia, the Scythians or the Cimmerians as the historical background, but none is certain, and Ezekiel seems to be making a symbol of an enemy from the far north. Josephus equates Magog with the Scythians (Antiquities 1.123). Revelation 20:8 turns 'Gog and Magog' into two nations at the four corners of the earth.

p: The Hebrew nesi rosh can mean 'chief leader' or 'the leader of Rosh'; the Russia reading depends on the second.
b: Nesi' rosh can be read two ways. If rosh is the ordinary word for 'head' or 'chief', it means 'chief leader' of Meshech and Tubal (the Masoretic Text's most natural reading; the Latin Vulgate has the Latin for 'head', capitis). If it is a name, it means 'leader of Rosh, Meshech and Tubal', and the Greek reads this way (archonta Rhōs). The identification of Rosh with Russia is traced to the Hebrew lexicon of Gesenius (as reported by Block); the Scofield Reference Bible's note on 38:2 and Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970) spread it. It rests on the second reading and on the similar sound of the names; the Rus' people enter history more than a thousand years after Ezekiel. Nasi is 'leader', not 'prince' (see 34:24). See also the variant.

p: Readers have named Gog as Goths, Turks and Russians; the text names none of them.
b: Ambrose took Gog to be the Goths (On the Christian Faith 2.16), a reading shaped by the Gothic threat to Rome in his day. Augustine refused to name peoples at all and read Gog and Magog as the nations of the whole earth against the church (City of God 20.11). Many Protestants of the sixteenth century, Luther among them, read Gog as the Ottoman Turks (Luther's 1530 preface to Ezekiel 38 and 39). From the nineteenth century, some read 'Rosh' as Russia, and the Scofield Reference Bible says this; Hal Lindsey popularized it in 1970. The Qur'an knows 'Yajuj and Majuj' behind a wall (Qur'an 18:94-99; 21:96). The range of identifications shows how open the picture has been to each age's fears.

t: Dragged out like a captured beast
p: Gog is drawn out with hooks: he comes because God brings him.
b: Hooks in the jaws drag a captured animal. The same picture was used of Pharaoh, the great crocodile, in 29:4, and of Sennacherib, who had a hook put in his nose and a bit in his mouth (2 Kings 19:28). The hook says that the army is not free: it only seems to be acting on its own plan (38:10-12). The LORD says three times in these chapters that he will bring Gog out (38:4, 16; 39:2). The picture is of an enemy led, and led to its end.

p: The list stretches to the edges of the known world: north, east, south and west.
b: Persia also appears in Tyre's army in 27:10; Cush is Nubia (southern Egypt), and Put is Libya, both named with Egypt in 30:5. Gomer and Beth-togarmah are in Anatolia and beyond (Genesis 10:2-3; 27:14), Sheba and Dedan are in Arabia, Tarshish is the far west (27:12, 15, 20, 22). Read together, the names run from the north to Persia in the east, to Africa in the south and to the Mediterranean in the west: a coalition of the whole world at its edges. Some of the same names appear in the table of nations (Genesis 10) and in the list of Tyre's trading partners (chapter 27).

a: In the last of the years
p: Acharit means 'end' or 'afterward'; the phrase need not mean the end of the world.
b: Acharit hashanim 'the end of the years' (here) and acharit hayyamim 'the end of the days' (38:16) are time phrases used throughout the Bible (Genesis 49:1; Numbers 24:14; Deuteronomy 4:30; Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5). Depending on the context they mean 'in later times' or 'in the days to come', and in the later prophets and Daniel they come to mean the final age. Commentators differ on where Ezekiel stands: some hear a distant future after the return from exile, others an end-time battle. The site renders the same phrase elsewhere 'in the last days' (Jeremiah 48:47; 49:39).

p: Gog expects an easy target; the picture is of a country at peace after the return.
b: Perazot are open, unwalled villages. Zechariah 2:4-5 promises Jerusalem will be 'inhabited as unwalled villages' with the LORD as a wall of fire around her; the same hope is behind this verse. Judah after the exile was a small province of villages, with Jerusalem's wall still to be built by Nehemiah. Gog's plan looks at this peace as weakness. Ezekiel 38:8, 11, 14 repeat 'safety' (betach) because that is the thing Gog does not understand.

p: Tabbur is the navel: the center from which the world was thought to extend.
b: Tabbur ha'arets is literally 'the navel of the earth'. It appears only once more in the Bible, in Judges 9:37. Ezekiel 5:5 already calls Jerusalem the center of the nations. Jewish writings made the idea a doctrine: Jubilees 8:19 and 1 Enoch 26:1 put the center of the earth at Zion, and later midrash repeats it. Ancient peoples often claimed a sacred site as the world's center (Delphi is the Greek example, and omphalos, 'navel', is the Greek word; the Greek of 38:12 itself says omphalos tes ges, 'the navel of the earth'). Gog thinks he is attacking a village; the text says he is attacking the center of the world.

p: Sheba, Dedan and Tarshish do not join Gog; they ask whether he has come to rob.
b: Sheba, Dedan and the traders of Tarshish are Tyre's trading partners (27:12, 15, 20, 22). They do not join the army. They ask whether Gog has come for loot, as if they want a share or at least understand. 'Strong young men' is kefirim, 'young lions', a word for the powerful leaders of a place. The Greek has 'Carthaginian traders' for the 'traders of Tarshish' (Swete), taking Tarshish to be Carthage in the west; the Latin keeps 'Tharsis'. Whether Tarshish was Spain, Sardinia or Carthage is debated.

t: At the end of the days
p: Acharit hayyamim: see the note at 38:8; the nations' purpose in this verse is that they will know the LORD.
b: Acharit hayyamim in 38:16 matches acharit hashanim in 38:8. The sentence gives the purpose: the LORD brings Gog 'so that the nations will know me, when I show my holiness through you before their eyes'. That purpose belongs to Ezekiel's repeated 'then they will know that I am the LORD'. It is hard to read the LORD as bringing an army to destruction to prove who he is. Readers explain it as judgment on arrogance, as a display of holiness before the world, or as a promise that Israel's security is final.

a: the one I mentioned long ago
p: No earlier prophet names Gog; the proposals include Jeremiah's foe from the north.
b: No book that survives names Gog before Ezekiel. Commentators propose that the 'servants, the prophets of Israel' are Jeremiah (the foe 'from the north', Jeremiah 6:22), Isaiah (the assault on Zion, Isaiah 14:24-27; 29:5-8), Joel (the northern army, Joel 2:20) or Zephaniah and Micah. The question is open. Some commentators treat the verse as an editor's comment that ties the Gog oracle to earlier prophecy. Others read the verse as Ezekiel's own way of saying that Gog is the fulfillment of what the prophets always said about the north.

p: A cosmic shaking is the usual sign of God's coming in judgment.
b: The earthquake that shakes the animals and the mountains (38:19-20) belongs with the pictures of God's coming at Sinai (Exodus 19:18), in Psalm 18:7 and in Haggai 2:6-7 ('I will shake the heavens and the earth'). Zechariah 14:4-5 splits the Mount of Olives. Revelation uses the same shaking at the seals, the trumpets and the bowls (Revelation 6:12; 8:5; 16:18). The same Hebrew word (ra'ash) is used of the rattling of the bones in 37:7.
r: Exodus 19:18; Psalm 18:7; Haggai 2:6-7; Zechariah 14:4-5; Revelation 6:12; Revelation 8:5; Revelation 16:18; 37:7

a: I will summon a sword against him on all my mountains
p: The Hebrew is awkward, and the Greek has a different text; the Plain English Translation takes it as a sword called on Israel's mountains.
b: Weqara'ti alav lekhol-harai kherev is, word for word, 'I will call against him, to all my mountains, a sword.' The odd part is that 'to all my mountains' stands between the verb and the thing called. The Plain English Translation reads it as a sword summoned against Gog on the mountains of Israel, where he falls (38:8; 39:2, 4). The Greek has no mountains and reads 'every terror' (panta phobon); see the variant. Whichever text is right, the next line is the same: the army turns on itself.
orig: וְקָרָאתִי עָלָיו לְכָל־הָרַי חֶרֶב (weqara'ti alav lekhol-harai kherev)

a: The sword of each man will be against his brother.
p: In holy war God sometimes makes an enemy army kill itself.
b: God turns an enemy army on itself in Judges 7:22 (Midianites at Gideon's trumpets), 1 Samuel 14:20 (Philistines) and 2 Chronicles 20:23 (Moab and Ammon at Jehoshaphat's praise). Haggai 2:22 and Zechariah 14:13 use the same picture of the last battle. The point is that the LORD wins without Israel's strength. Notice that Israel does nothing in this chapter; the next chapter will give it work, burning and burying (39:9-16).

p: The punishment recalls Sodom and the plagues of Egypt; Revelation 20:10 has 'fire and sulfur'.
b: Rain, hailstones, fire and sulfur recall the destruction of Sodom (Genesis 19:24) and the hail and fire on Egypt (Exodus 9:23-25). Psalm 11:6 says God will rain coals, fire and sulfur on the wicked. Revelation 20:9-10 has fire from heaven that 'ate them up' and a 'lake of fire and sulfur' for the devil, and Revelation 19:17-21 takes the next chapter's feast of birds. Ezekiel's fire is a judgment on the battlefield; it is not a place of punishment after death.

a: swing you around and push you forward
p: The Hebrew verb is rare and its meaning is uncertain; the KJV's 'leave but the sixth part' is a guess from 'six'.
b: Shishshe'tikha is rare and its root is not clear. The KJV has 'leave but the sixth part of thee', reading it from shesh 'six'. Others derive it from shasha 'to lead, to drive' and render it 'drive you on'. The Greek (Swete) has synaxo se kai kathodegeso se kai anabibo se ep' eschatou tou borra, 'I will gather you and guide you and bring you up to the far north', a different picture. The Plain English Translation chooses 'push you forward' because of the context of an army led where God wishes.

p: Revelation draws on this chapter but changes the picture; the churches and synagogue read the link differently.
b: Ezekiel 39:6 sends fire on Magog and on those who live safely on the islands, the far coasts. In Revelation 20:8-9: "Gog and Magog, to gather them for the battle. Their number is like the sand of the sea." (Revelation 20:8). Fire also comes from heaven there (Revelation 20:9). The differences are real: in Ezekiel, Gog is a ruler and Magog his land, the battle is on Israel's mountains and the burying lasts months; in Revelation, Gog and Magog are nations at the four corners of the earth, and the battle comes after the thousand years. The synagogue reads Ezekiel 38:18-39:16 on the Sabbath of Sukkot, and the Talmud speaks of the war of Gog and Magog (Berakhot 7b). See the 'Where Christians differ' card.

p: Seven is the number of fullness; some readers take the years and months literally.
b: The weapons are so many that the people will use them for fuel for seven years (39:9-10), and the burying will take seven months (39:12). Seven stands for completeness, a whole round of time, as in Ezekiel 3:15 and the seven days of 43:25-26. Some readers take the numbers as symbols, others as literal lengths of time. Isaiah 9:5 has the same idea of burning the gear of war. The text gives no more help.

p: The name means 'the travelers', and some read 'Abarim', the mountains east of the Dead Sea.
b: Gei ha'overim is 'the Valley of the Travelers' or 'those who pass'. The word is a play on the verb 'avar 'to pass', used again and again in 39:11-15 (travelers, passers). Some commentators prefer ha'abarim, the Abarim mountains east of the Dead Sea (Numbers 27:12; 33:47), because 'east of the sea' puts it near there. The Greek gives 'a famous place, a burial ground in Israel' and calls it polyandrion, 'the mass grave of those who came' by the sea, and also names the city Polyandrion (39:16). 'Hamon-gog' means 'the horde of Gog', and 'Hamonah' (39:16) means 'horde' or 'multitude'.

p: Contact with a dead body made a person and land unclean; the burying cleanses the land.
b: A corpse made people unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11-16), and an unburied body defiled the land (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). With so many dead, the whole land would be unclean for a long time. The seven months of burying, with men who search for any bone left over (39:14-15), are the cleansing. The picture also shows the LORD's care for a holy land and a Temple that Ezekiel is about to describe (40-48).

a: the sacrifice I am slaughtering for you
p: God calls a feast of battle dead: an old picture in Isaiah, Zephaniah and Revelation 19.
b: The slaughter of an enemy is called a zevach, a sacrifice, in Isaiah 34:6, Jeremiah 46:10 and Zephaniah 1:7. The guests are the birds and wild animals. Revelation 19:17-18 takes up this scene, as an angel who "cried out with a loud voice to all the birds flying high overhead" (Revelation 19:17) to the great supper of God. The meal is the reverse of the one in 34:25-28, where wild animals lose their threat.

p: The sacrifice's animals stand for the leaders and soldiers; compare Psalm 22:12 and Amos 4:1.
b: Rams, lambs, goats, bulls and the fattened animals of Bashan are the sacrificial animals, but the text says they are the warriors and 'the leaders of the earth'. Bashan was famous for fat cattle (Psalm 22:12; Amos 4:1; Deuteronomy 32:14). In chapter 34, the leaders were 'rams and male goats' (34:17), so the image runs back to the shepherd chapter. Here the strong are the ones eaten.

a: I will put my glory among the nations
p: The glory that left the Temple (10-11) is set among the nations, then returns to the Temple (43:1-5).
b: The 'glory' (kavod) of the LORD is his weighty presence, the blaze Ezekiel saw at the river Chebar (1:28). It left the Temple before the fall (10:18-19; 11:22-23), and it will return to the Temple by the east gate (43:1-5). Here the glory is shown to the nations by what God does to Gog. The Plain English Translation never renders kavod as 'weight' or 'honor'; the root meaning 'heavy' is in a note only.

a: went into exile for their guilt
t: The exile explained to the nations
p: The nations had the wrong idea about the exile; God now corrects it.
b: In 36:20 the nations concluded that the LORD was too weak to keep his people in the land. Here they are told the truth: the exile was punishment for Israel's unfaithfulness (ma'al, 'acting unfaithfully'), and God hid his face. The view of exile as just punishment shapes the books of Kings and Chronicles, and it is the theodicy of Ezekiel. The next lines (39:25-29) turn to restoration. Readers who think this puts the whole blame on Israel note 39:26, where Israel bears its shame, and 39:29, where the Spirit ends the hiding.

p: God hiding his face is the opposite of the blessing in Numbers 6:25.
b: To hide the face is to withdraw help and favor. Deuteronomy 31:17-18 foretells it as the result of Israel's turning to other gods, and Psalm 27:9, 30:7 and Isaiah 54:8 pray or promise that it will end. The priestly blessing asks the LORD to make his face shine on his people (Numbers 6:25). Ezekiel uses the phrase here and in 39:24, 29 as a frame: the hiding begins with exile and ends with the Spirit.

p: The phrase means to reverse a bad condition; the old translation 'bring back the captivity' is a guess.
b: Shuv shevut (the written form is shevit) means to turn someone's condition around. The KJV has 'bring again the captivity', but the same phrase is used where there was no captivity (Job 42:10, where the LORD 'turned' Job's fortunes), so the Plain English Translation says 'turn the fortunes around', as it does in Job and Jeremiah. It is a favorite of Jeremiah and Ezekiel's restoration oracles (Jeremiah 29:14; 30:3, 18; Ezekiel 16:53; 29:14; 39:25). The Greek has apostrephō aichmalōsian, 'turn back the captivity'.

p: The Hebrew says they will bear their shame; some read 'forget', and some English versions do.
b: The Leningrad Codex spells the word venasu, with no aleph. That spelling can be read two ways: from nasa', 'they will bear' their shame and their unfaithfulness (the usual full spelling would be venas'u), or from nashah, 'they will forget', which suits a joyful restoration, and some commentators and English translations read it that way. The Greek (Swete) agrees with 'bear': 'they will take their dishonor'. The Plain English Translation keeps 'bear', the Masoretic Text and the Greek, as a sober reading: restored people remember, and they bear what they did, safely and without fear.

a: I have poured my Spirit out on the house of Israel
p: The book of promises ends with the Spirit poured out; Joel, Acts and Zechariah use the same image.
b: The 'pouring out' of the Spirit (shafakh) is a rare image of overflowing: Isaiah 32:15 (until the Spirit is poured out from on high), Isaiah 44:3, Zechariah 12:10, Joel 2:28-29. Acts 2:17-18 says Pentecost fulfills Joel, and Acts 10:45 shows the gift poured out on the Gentiles. In Ezekiel the pouring is the final proof that the hiding is over: God does not turn away from people in whom his Spirit lives. The promise joins 36:27 and 37:14.
